scenes.title: Call the point before the ball lands
The fast tier wins every month
The backtest, in sample and out

captions.text: This is a real table tennis rally, from a game our model never saw in training.
It calls this shot a miss 408 milliseconds before the ball gets there.
That is our longest call on held-out games. The median is 25 milliseconds, and it called 8 of 41 test misses early.
Courtside asks what that head start is worth on a prediction market, and what we can prove.
When a point ends, the news spreads in tiers.
Ball tracking knows before the bounce. Our vision model takes about 158 milliseconds per call in a laptop benchmark; we have no courtside camera.
Market makers reprice about 1.3 seconds before the official point stamp. ESPN's live score trails the book by about 28 seconds.
Slower tiers trade against stale prices. The gap persists because speed costs money, and capacity is small.
A small group of wallets trades in the first three seconds after a point.
Thirty seconds later, net of fees, they are up in 11 of 11 months, including 3 of 3 out of sample. Everyone else is down in 11.
Copying them three seconds later loses in 11 of 11. The edge goes to whoever is first.
So we tested whether vision could get there.
On held-out table tennis games, it tracks the ball and calls misses before contact.
Fifty milliseconds out, it made 11 calls, all correct. The 95% lower bound on precision is 74 percent.
It catches 27 percent of misses that early, and leaves the rest alone.
We have no licensed tennis footage, so this replay is simulated physics.
In simulation, a 340 frame per second tracker calls it out 200 milliseconds before the bounce, and reads the spin from the flight.
On the right is a real Polymarket tape: fast-tier wallets traded within seconds of the point.
Version two trades only at the fast tier's own fill prices, after fees.
In sample, February to August: 1.38 cents a share, Sharpe 14.5, worst drawdown 2.0 percent.
Out of sample, a window we had already seen: 0.60 cents, Sharpe 6.7.
Double the fees, and out of sample turns negative: −0.34 cents.
We tried thousands of configurations, so we deflate the Sharpe ratio.
In sample it is 0.997, even counting all 3,410 trials.
The 40-day out-of-sample window does not survive that. It falls to 0.075.
Probability of backtest overfitting on the 24-variant grid: 15 percent picking by Sharpe, 42 percent with our own selection rule.
Unseen markets passed in sample and failed out of sample. The original copy strategy lost 36 thousand dollars on its blind window, and the market-making variant failed its blind test.
The frozen tier-zero version failed its blind tests too. In table tennis markets we detected no fast tier.
The blind forward test runs once, planned for 2026-10-04 11:30 UTC. Every look at out-of-sample data is logged: 65 entries at render time.
What does vision buy? This part is a counterfactual.
It assumes a licensed feed and a courtside camera we did not buy, with parameters we measured.
In sample, 1.10 cents a share, Sharpe 11.4. Out of sample, 0.58 cents, Sharpe 7.3.
The sign hinges on how fast the market reprices after the bounce, which we have not measured.
Under the stamp reading, if that takes less than 1.1 seconds, the edge is gone. Our pre-registered estimate, 0.68 seconds, falls in that zone.
A frozen version then failed its blind tests on unseen markets.
The market-data and paper-trading legs run on live Polymarket order books, paper only.
In a 60 second check it read 7,785 book messages across 27 markets,
at a median feed latency of 65 milliseconds, with 0 mismatches and 0 orders sent.
The full chain, from vision call to paper order, ran on a recorded book. A live paper session started on 2026-10-03 at 20:48 UTC; at render time it was still warming up, so it had not quoted yet.
In sample, a gross edge of 282 dollars a day loses 86 to taker fees, leaving 196.
Central fixed costs, mostly a data licence, are 167 a day. That leaves 29 in sample, and a loss out of sample.
Before fixed costs, out of sample is still positive at 34 thousand dollars of capital, and negative by 54 thousand.
Kill switches stop trading on a drawdown, a stale feed, or a fee change.
Everything here is paper trading. No real money was traded.
We bought no official ATP or WTA data feed, and no trading result uses one. Free public score pages were recorded only to time their lag.
The code is public. One command replays the paper engine on recorded books in seconds. Two more rebuild every table from public data, in one to two hours.
Every number in this video is listed with its source file in the video manifest.
